sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equation is already fully factored. Note that the discriminant of [MATH: x^2 + 5 = 0] is

[MATH: \mathcal{D}= 0^2 - 4(1)(5) = -20 < 0,] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the function [MATH: f(x)] has a single root at [MATH: x=4.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by plugging the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation: [MATH: y|= (1)/(5)(0 − 4)(0^{2} + 5); = (1)/(5)(− 4)(5); = − 4]

So, the curve:

  • has a [MATH: y]-intercept at the point [MATH: (0,-4),]

  • passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=4,] and

  • has no more [MATH: x]-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 24,] sketch the curve [MATH: y = f(x).]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 24,] sketch the curve [MATH: y = f(x).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x),] so [MATH: (x-3)] divides [MATH: f(x)] with zero remainder. To begin factoring [MATH: f(x),] we can divide it by [MATH: (x-3)] using synthetic division: [MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 3|1|1|− 4|− 24; 3|12|24; 1|4|8|0]

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac{f(x)}{x-3} = x^2 + 4x + 8,] which means that

[MATH: f(x) = (x-3)(x^2 + 4x + 8).]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of [MATH: x^2 + 4x + 8 = 0] is [MATH: \mathcal{D}= 4^2 - 4(1)(8) = -16 < 0,]

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that [MATH: f(x)] has a single root at [MATH: x=3.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by substituting the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:

[MATH: y|= 0^{3} + 0^{2} − 4(0) − 24 = − 24.]

So, the curve:

  • has a [MATH: y]-intercept at [MATH: (0,-24),]

  • passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=3,] and

  • has no more [MATH: x]-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows (figure not to scale):

[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 4|− 1|4|− 4|16; − 4|0|− 16; − 1|0|− 4|0]

Therefore, [MATH: (f(x))/(x − 4)|= − x^{2} − 4; = − (x^{2} + 4),]

which means that [MATH: f(x) = -(x-4)(x^2 + 4).]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of [MATH: x^2 + 4 = 0] is [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0^2 - 4(1)(4) = - 16 < 0,]

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that [MATH: f(x)] has a single root at [MATH: x=4.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by substituting the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:

[MATH: y = -(0)^3 + 4(0)^2 - 4(0) + 16 = 16]

  • passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=4,] and

  • has no more [MATH: x]-intercepts.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The graph of any cubic function [MATH: y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d,] where [MATH: a >0,] has a characteristic inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape, with [MATH: y]-values ranging from [MATH: -\infty] to [MATH: +\infty.] This means that every such function has at least one real root and at most three distinct roots.

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x^3-3x^2 +3x-1.] First, we need to find the roots, so we set [MATH: y=0] and solve. Noting that the polynomial is a perfect cube, we find

Content:
[MATH: x^{3} − 3x^{2} + 3x − 1|= 0; (x − 1)^{3}|= 0.]

Content:
So we get one real root [MATH: x=1,] which has multiplicity [MATH: 3.]

Content:
At a root of multiplicity [MATH: 3,] the graph becomes tangent (i.e., lies parallel) to the [MATH: x]-axis and crosses the [MATH: x]-axis.

Content:
Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9c0a169392c0e232fdea24674564fcbb]

---

Item 2 — Example: Graphing a Factored Cubic Curve with a Positive Leading Coefficient

Example Prompt:
Sketch the curve [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{5}(x-4)(x^2 + 5).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equation is already fully factored. Note that the discriminant of [MATH: x^2 + 5 = 0] is

[MATH: \mathcal{D}= 0^2 - 4(1)(5) = -20 < 0,]
which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the function [MATH: f(x)] has a single root at [MATH: x=4.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by plugging the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:
[MATH: y|= (1)/(5)(0 − 4)(0^{2} + 5); = (1)/(5)(− 4)(5); = − 4]

So, the curve:

- has a [MATH: y]-intercept at the point [MATH: (0,-4),]
- passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=4,] and
- has no more [MATH: x]-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/3567a9f10d8334c4ac37cd1451c1de94]

Item 5 — Example: Graphing an Expanded Cubic Curve with a Positive Leading Coefficient

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 24,] sketch the curve [MATH: y = f(x).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x),] so [MATH: (x-3)] divides [MATH: f(x)] with zero remainder. To begin factoring [MATH: f(x),] we can divide it by [MATH: (x-3)] using synthetic division:
[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 3|1|1|− 4|− 24; 3|12|24; 1|4|8|0]

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac{f(x)}{x-3} = x^2 + 4x + 8,]
which means that

[MATH: f(x) = (x-3)(x^2 + 4x + 8).]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of [MATH: x^2 + 4x + 8 = 0] is
[MATH: \mathcal{D}= 4^2 - 4(1)(8) = -16 < 0,]

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that [MATH: f(x)] has a single root at [MATH: x=3.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by substituting the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:

[MATH: y|= 0^{3} + 0^{2} − 4(0) − 24 = − 24.]

So, the curve:

- has a [MATH: y]-intercept at [MATH: (0,-24),]
- passes through the [MATH: x]-axis at the single root [MATH: x=3,] and
- has no more [MATH: x]-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows (figure not to scale):

[IMG: /graphics/c2c780ca8947108a4000dda33521f78c]
